# Plot format and identity

::: {.doc-lead}
Understand the files, stable IDs and data contracts used by Flux and other consumers.
:::

## The file bundle {#the-file-bundle}

Saving a plot named `growth` with `fp.save` writes three files side by side: the artwork,
a semantic index and a provenance recipe.

### `growth.svg` — visible artwork {#growth.svg-visible-artwork}
The SVG opens independently in a browser or vector editor. fluxplot adds two pieces of information to each meaningful element:

- a **stable, meaningful `id`** — `control.line`, `control.point.3`, `axis.x.title`, `legend`;
- **`data-*` attributes** carrying role + identity (+ the datum value, for convenience):

```xml
<g id="control.line" data-role="line" data-series="control"><path d="…"/></g>
…
<use id="control.point.3" data-role="point" data-series="control"
     data-index="3" data-x="12" data-y="0.41" x="182.05" y="103.5"/>
```

Text stays as real, editable `<text>` (axis titles, tick labels) — not outlined to paths — so it can be
restyled and read.

### `growth.fluxplot.json` — the semantic index {#growth.fluxplot.json-the-semantic-index}
A sidecar that **points into the SVG by id** and adds everything SVG can't naturally express. It never
duplicates geometry (no path data, no bounding boxes — those live authoritatively in the SVG). It
holds:

```jsonc
{
  "spec": "fluxplot/manifest", "schemaVersion": "0.4.0", "plotType": "line",
  "axes": [{
    "x": { "scale": "linear", "domain": [-1.2, 25.2],
           "anchors": [{"data": -1.2, "svg": 57.6}, {"data": 25.2, "svg": 414.72}] },
    "y": { "scale": "log", "base": 10, "domain": [0.0158, 2.6767],
           "anchors": [{"data": 0.0158, "svg": 307.6}, {"data": 2.6767, "svg": 41.5}] }
  }],
  "series": [{ "id": "control", "kind": "line",
               "svg": {"line": "control.line", "points": "control.points"},
               "data": { "x": [0,4,8,…], "y": [0.02,0.05,0.13,…] },
               "points": [ … {"index": 3, "svgId": "control.point.3",
                              "x": 12, "y": 0.41} … ] }],
  "build": { "order": ["axis.x","axis.y","gridlines","control.line","treatment.line",
                       "control.points","treatment.points","legend",
                       "significance-bracket.0"],
             "presets": { "line": {"animation": "draw-on"},
                          "point": {"animation": "stagger-in"} } },
  "layout": { "version": 1, "supported": true, "reasons": [],
              "engine": { "kind": "constrained", … }, "axes": [ … ],
              "texts": { … }, "fonts": { … }, "frames": { … } }
}
```

Flux uses this index to select named parts and interpret their data; the `layout` block (schema
0.4) is what lets it [resize a plot without Python](#layout-capture).

### Plot types and payloads {#plot-types-and-payloads}

`schemaVersion` is the manifest schema the writing fluxplot emitted — `"0.4.0"` for fluxplot 0.4
(`fp.SPEC_VERSION`); the recipe's `$id` carries the same number. Each schema version is additive over
the last, so a consumer written for 0.3.2 still reads a 0.4.0 manifest.

`plotType` is a one-word hint for a consumer's gallery and defaults: the first of `meanmark`,
`fluxbox`, `hexmatrix`, `image`, `regression`, `kde`, `line`, `scatter`, `bar`, `errorbar`,
`area`, `box`, `violin`, `heatmap`, `contour`, `contourf`, `surface` found among the tagged marks,
else `plot`. fluxplot 0.4 replaced the glowbar with the [meanmark](/docs/fluxplot-api.html#meanmark),
so `"glowbar"` is no longer written; manifests saved earlier keep it.

Beyond `data`, a series entry carries an additive **payload** named after the helper that drew it,
holding exactly the numbers that were drawn so no consumer re-derives them from pixels:

| payload | written by | contents |
|---|---|---|
| `meanmark` | `fp.meanmark` | per category (`part: "summary"`): `n`, `mean`, `meanKind` (`arithmetic`), `sd`, `sem`, `interval` (`ci` / `sem` / `sd` / `range` / a callable's name), `confidence` (CI only, else `null`), `low`, `high` (`null` for a single observation), `x`, `y`, `categoryPosition`, `orientation`, `scale`, `groupColor`, `palette`; per unit (`part: "unit"`): `units`, `unit`, `categories`, `colors` |
| `fluxbox` | `fp.fluxbox` | per category: `n`, `mean`, `median`, `sd`, `sem`, `q1`, `q3`, `iqr`, `whis`, `whiskerLow`, `whiskerHigh`, `outliers`, `x`, `groupColor`, `palette`; on a log axis also `scale: "log"` and `meanKind: "geometric"`; unit entries as above |
| `hexmatrix` | `fp.hexmatrix` | the lattice and bins drawn, the statistic and the dropped-point count, beside the usual `field` colour payload |
| `bar`, `band`, `uncertainty`, `step`, `stem` | `fp.bar` / `barh`, `fp.area` / `band`, `fp.errorbar`, `fp.step`, `fp.stem` | bar keys by category and orientation; `{x, y1, y2}` or `{x, lo, hi, what}`; `xerr` / `yerr` broadcast to the points with `errShape`; `where`; the baseline |
| `distribution` | `fp.hist` | `binEdges`, `counts` |
| `regression`, `kde` | `fp.regression`, `fp.kde` | the fit (`kind`, `degree`, `coefficients`, `r2`, `p`, `n`, `ci`); the grid, density and bandwidth |
| `field`, `image`, `surface` | `fp.heatmap` / `contour` / `contourf`, `fp.image`, `fp.surface` | the scalar field's colour scale (a `colorScales[]` entry; the values with `include_values` or `value_raster`); the image's `shape`, `channels` (name, LUT, display range, scale), `composite`, `origin`, `extent`, `pixelSize`; the surface map's kind, categories and range |

Raw observations are never implied by a summary: `box`, `violin`, `hist`, `heatmap` and the
signature plots record sample values only when the call asked for it (`include_values=True`).

### `growth.recipe.json` — the provenance {#growth.recipe.json-the-provenance}
The script (auto-discovered, or recorded explicitly), the parameters, references (+ hashes) of the
input data, and a `provenance` block (script hash, interpreter, package versions, git state when
available). Enough to **re-run the plot here** — which is what makes "rerun Figure 6d with a
Mann-Whitney test" a real operation. All host-varying material lives here, never in the SVG/manifest.

A plot made in a notebook cell has no script to re-run. `fp.save(..., recipe={"notebook": path,
"cell": "fig-growth"})` records it honestly: `provenance.scriptDiscovery: "notebook"` and a
`notebook: {path, cell, sha256}` block, with no `command`. In a live kernel the notebook is
detected from what the host states outright — `$QUARTO_DOCUMENT_PATH`, or the
`__vsc_ipynb_file__` / `__session__` globals — and never guessed from the working directory.

### Consistency between the three files {#consistency-between-the-three-files}
The manifest records `artifact.svgSha256` — the checksum of the final SVG bytes. `save` stages all
three files and commits them with atomic per-file renames (SVG → manifest → recipe), so a watcher
never sees a partially written file, and a stale SVG/manifest pair is *detectable* via the checksum
rather than silently misinterpreted.

**Why split SVG and manifest?** Because they answer different questions in the representation each is
good at. The SVG answers *"how does it look and which part is which?"* — that belongs in a vector
tree. The manifest answers *"what does it mean and how does it move?"* — nested numeric data,
coordinate transforms, choreography — which fit naturally in
JSON. The authority rule keeps them from drifting: **geometry is authoritative in the SVG; data,
coordinate-mapping, and choreography are authoritative in the manifest; identity + role appear in both
as the join key.**

## Export pipeline {#export-pipeline}

fluxplot uses matplotlib's one real hook from "an artist" to "a named SVG element":
`artist.set_gid("control.line")` makes matplotlib's SVG backend wrap that artist's output in
`<g id="control.line">…</g>`. The pipeline in `save()` is:

1. **Assign deterministic gids.** Walk the marks you tagged and give each a semantic id (`ids.py`).
2. **Auto-tag the scaffold.** Name the axes, tick labels, legend, and title so you never have to.
3. **Capture coordinates.** Read each axis's real transform and record the data↔pixel mapping + scale
   (see below).
4. **Render deterministically.** Save to SVG with the determinism knobs set (see below).
5. **Inject `data-*` + canonicalize.** matplotlib writes only `id`, never arbitrary attributes — so a
   post-render pass (`postprocess.py`, via lxml) finds each element **by the id we ourselves set** and
   adds `data-role`/`data-series`/… , splits the points group into addressable per-point elements, and
   strips volatile metadata.
6. **Emit the manifest and recipe.**

> **Is step 5 reverse-engineering?** No — and the distinction is the whole
> point. Reverse-engineering means looking at an anonymous `<path>` and *guessing from its colour or
> shape* that it's the control line. Here, **we set `id="control.line"` before rendering**, so the
> post-pass is an *exact structural join on an id we authored* plus annotation with values our code
> already had. Nothing is inferred from pixels. It's serialization, not divination.

### Per-point addressability {#per-point-addressability}
"The 4th point of the control series" needs each point to be its *own* element. matplotlib draws a
set of markers as one artist: a marker glyph defined once in `<defs>`, then one `<use>` per point in
data order. fluxplot's post-pass enumerates those `<use>` children and stamps each with
`id="control.point.k"` + `data-index`/`data-x`/`data-y`. (If matplotlib ever culls off-axis points and
the count stops matching the data, fluxplot detects the mismatch and keeps the group addressable
rather than mislabel indices.)

### Heavy layers are rasterized by default {#heavy-layers-are-rasterized-by-default}
An artist becomes as many SVG nodes as it draws primitives. A `LineCollection` built from per-edge
segments — the ordinary way to draw an SWC reconstruction or a graph — emits **one `<path>` per
segment**, and a `scatter` emits **one `<use>` per point**. At real data scale that is 10⁴–10⁵ nodes
in a single panel, and consumers inline that markup as live DOM, where it is ruinous. (Measured: a
14-panel figure carrying three neuron reconstructions and 8.7k-point scatters reached 260,907 nodes
and ~390 ms per pan frame — about 2.5 fps.)

So `fp.save` rasterizes any artist over `raster_threshold` primitives (default 800) into a single
embedded `<image>` at `raster_dpi` (default 600), and says so:

```
fluxplot: 'medoid' — rasterized 2 heavy layer(s) at 600 dpi:
axon.x-morphology (72,586 primitives), dendrite.x-morphology (4,199 primitives).
Axes, ticks, labels and legend stay vector.
Pass force_vectors=True to keep everything as vectors.
```

**Only the heavy layer is rasterized.** Axes, spines, ticks, tick labels, the legend, annotations and
every lighter series stay fully vector and fully editable — this is matplotlib's own `set_rasterized`
applied per artist, which is what journals expect for dense scatter and line art anyway. The
rasterized layer **keeps its id, its `data-role`/`data-series` and its manifest entry**, so it stays
addressable as a whole; only *per-point* ids are unavailable, because a rasterized cloud has no
per-point nodes. `SaveResult.rasterized` lists what was rasterized and the manifest marks those
entries `"rasterized": true`.

On a real morphology panel: **13.42 MB / 76,852 nodes → 0.06 MB / 67 nodes**, rendering
pixel-indistinguishable (mean channel difference 0.11/255).

Opt out with `fp.save(..., force_vectors=True)` or `FLUXPLOT_FORCE_VECTORS=1`; the heavy layers are
then still reported, as a warning naming them and their node cost. A per-artist
`set_rasterized(False)` does **not** override the default — that is matplotlib's factory setting
rather than a considered choice, and silently emitting an unusable SVG is the failure this exists to
prevent. `force_vectors` is how you say you meant it.

### Determinism — the same plot always produces the same bytes {#determinism-the-same-plot-always-produces-the-same-bytes}
This is non-negotiable, because **morphing, diffing, and regeneration all break if ids or structure
wobble between runs.** fluxplot pins the sources of nondeterminism:

- `svg.hashsalt` is fixed (otherwise matplotlib salts every clip-path / glyph id with a fresh UUID);
- `svg.fonttype='none'` keeps text as `<text>` (the default outlines glyphs into font-version-dependent
  path data, *and* makes labels un-restylable);
- the SVG date metadata is dropped, path-simplification is pinned, and the JSON is written canonically
  (sorted keys, fixed float precision).

Result: same input → byte-identical SVG and manifest. Timestamps and content hashes (which *must*
vary) live only in the recipe, so the SVG/manifest stay stable for diffs and morphs.

### Coordinate capture — why the manifest stores "anchors" {#coordinate-capture-why-the-manifest-stores-anchors}
A morph that moves a point from value 2 to value 8 on a **log** axis must travel correctly, which is
impossible from pixels alone. So per axis fluxplot stores the scale type and two `(data, svg)` anchor
pairs. A consumer interpolates between them — linearly, or in log space for a log axis — and gets the
exact pixel position for any data value, **without ever reconstructing matplotlib's transform.** Two
anchors + a scale type is the complete, portable contract. (fluxplot computes them with a
dpi-invariant fraction method that round-trips *exactly* against the positions matplotlib actually
emits.)

### Layout capture — resizing without rerunning Python {#layout-capture}
Schema 0.4.0 adds one additive block, `layout`, captured after the final SVG-renderer draw while
the layout is frozen. It is a set of constraints and measurements, never a second drawing: the SVG
remains the only authority for geometry. With it a consumer such as Flux can reflow a placed plot to a
new physical size with no browser text measurement and no Python — the axes and data areas resize,
data follows each axes' affine, numeric ticks are recomputed, and glyphs, typography and stroke
widths keep their point sizes. The block records:

- `figure` — the size in points and the ids of `suptitle` / `supxlabel` / `supylabel`;
- `engine` — the layout engine in force: `none` with the figure's `subplotpars`, `tight` with its
  pads and `rect`, or `constrained` with `wPad` / `hPad` / `wSpace` / `hSpace` / `rect`;
- `grids` — every GridSpec: rows, columns, width and height ratios, spacing, and the parent slot of
  a nested grid;
- `axes` and `colorbars` — per axes: its grid `slot` or inset bounds, `position` and
  `initialPosition`, `initialDomain` and `dataLim`, the `aspect` / `adjustable` / `anchor` /
  `boxAspect` rules, twin and shared axes, the title slots, `axisStyle` (tick direction, lengths and
  pads, label pads, fonts, which sides are drawn) and `ticking` — the major and minor locator and
  formatter as parameters (`maxn`, `multiple`, `log`, `fixed`, `category`, `date`, …; `scalar`,
  `log-sci`, `percent`, `str-method`, …) with the tick values and labels actually drawn and a
  `retick` flag saying whether new ticks may be computed. Colorbars add their parent axes,
  location, orientation, fraction, shrink and pad;
- `legends` — owner, requested and resolved `loc`, anchor box, size and, for `loc="best"`, the
  collision data matplotlib used to place it;
- `texts` — for every text part: bounding box, anchor point, alignment, rotation and font;
- `fonts` — each distinct font with its ascent and descent, the advance of every digit and sign
  character, and the mathtext metrics of exponent labels, measured by matplotlib's own SVG font
  engine at 72 dpi;
- `frames` — the coordinate frame of every part: `data`, `axes`, `figure`, `blend` (one data axis,
  one axes fraction), `image`, `offset` and `arrow` for annotations, `axis` / `title` / `legend` for
  scaffold, and `glyph` for point-sized geometry anchored to data — scatter markers (`anchorsPt`),
  fluxbox boxes (`box`: ends and notch in data, width and cut in points) and meanmark circles, arms
  and caps (`mark`: position, mean, bound, radius and cap length in points).

<figure class="doc-figure doc-clip"><video poster="/assets/media/docs/clips/reflow-resize.png" width="1400" height="1000" muted loop playsinline autoplay controls preload="metadata" aria-label="A fluxplot line plot placed in a figure is dragged narrower; Flux re-solves its layout from the manifest so the axes shrink while text and strokes keep their point sizes."><source src="/assets/media/docs/clips/reflow-resize.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video><figcaption>Flux reflows the plot from the layout block: axes and data re-solve, typography keeps its point size, and no Python runs.</figcaption></figure>

`supported` is `true` only when `reasons` is empty. Layouts the capture cannot describe record a
named refusal and save normally — the plot simply cannot be reflowed, and a consumer falls back to
stretching it: `subfigures`; `3d`; `projection:<name>` (polar and other non-rectilinear axes);
`layout:compressed` (constrained layout with `compress=True`); `layout:custom` (a custom layout
engine); `text:usetex:<id>`; `transform:custom:<id>` and `transform:annotation:<id>` (an artist or
annotation endpoint in a transform that is neither data, axes nor figure); `transform:secondary-axis:<axes>`
(a secondary axis whose conversion is not affine); `axes-locator:<axes>`; and
`ticks:no-template:<axes>.<axis>` (a dynamic major locator that drew no ticks, so there is no SVG tick
to clone). Date, category and custom-formatted ticks reposition without being recomputed.

The inputs — axes positions, domains and subplot parameters — are taken before the layout draw and
reused on repeated saves, so saving the same figure twice stays byte-identical even when a draw
adjusts limits or spacing. Plots saved by fluxplot 0.3 and earlier carry no `layout` block;
regenerate them with fluxplot ≥ 0.4 to make them reflowable. In Flux, see
[True physical size](/docs/semantic-plots.html#true-physical-size) and
[Resizing a figure](/docs/figure-layout.html#resizing-a-figure).

## Semantic IDs: the universal join key {#semantic-ids-the-universal-join-key}

Ids are **derived from meaning**, not random — a dotted path of `[a-z0-9-]` segments:

```
control.line          control.point.3        axis.x.title       axis.x.tick.2
legend                annotation.peak        reference-line.threshold        panel.a
```

The same id is simultaneously the SVG `id`, the manifest key, the handle a caption or animation step
refers to, and a coordinate in "meaning space" (`role=point, series=control, index=3`). Making it
**deterministic** is what lets four different operations work:

- **Durable references** — a restyle, a caption, or an animation attached to `control.line` survives the
  plot being **regenerated with new data**: the line is still "the control line" even though its shape
  changed, because it has the same id.
- **Morphing** — match parts across two versions of a plot by id, then tween.
- **Legible diffs** — a regenerated plot produces a meaningful git diff instead of noise.
- **Addressing** — humans and agents name a part the same way the file does.

(matplotlib's own ids use underscores and hex hashes and never contain dots, so fluxplot's dotted
namespace is provably disjoint from anything it autogenerates.)

A series name becomes its id segment by a deterministic slug: accents folded, Greek letters and
`µ` / `°` / `%` spelled out (`α` → `alpha`, `37 °C` → `37-degc`), super- and subscripts flattened
(`CO₂` → `co2`), lowercase, spaces to `-`. When dropping characters would let two names collide
(`IL-6 (pg/mL)` vs `IL-6 [pg/mL]`), a six-hex-digit hash of the name is appended, so distinct names
stay distinct and stable. Spines are named by side (`axis.x.spine.bottom`, `axis.y.spine.left`).
When a rule changes an id an older fluxplot emitted, the manifest's `idAliases` maps the old id (or
a series' old root) to the new one for one minor version, so a consumer resolves saved overrides
through it instead of losing them.

Two orthogonal axes of labeling make this work: **role** = *what kind of thing it is* (`line`,
`point`, `axis-title`) and **identity** = *which one* (`series=control`, `index=3`). Animation targets
by role ("draw every `line`"); a caption targets by identity ("the `treatment` series"); a journal
restyle targets by role across the whole figure ("every `axis-title` → 8pt").

## The role vocabulary {#the-role-vocabulary}

The part names aren't ad hoc — they're the **Grammar of Graphics** (the model behind ggplot2 and
Vega-Lite): a plot is *data → marks + scales + guides + annotations*. fluxplot's core roles (schema 0.4):

- **Containers:** `figure`, `panel`, `plot-area`, `legend`, `colorbar`, `title`, `subtitle`
- **Scaffold / guides:** `axis`, `spine`, `tick`, `tick-label`, `tick-offset` (the shared `×10ⁿ` offset text), `axis-title`, `gridline`, `background`, `legend-title`, `legend-entry`, `legend-swatch`, `legend-label`, `annotation-arrow`, `colorbar-divider`
- **Data marks:** `series`, `line`, `point`, `bar`, `area`, `errorbar`, `box`, `violin`, `contour`, `image`, `mesh`, `pane`, `scalebar`
- **Composite sub-parts:** `whisker`, `cap`, `flier`, `median`, `mean`, `segment`
- **Overlays:** `annotation`, `reference-line`, `highlight-region`, `significance-bracket`, `label`, `caption`
- **Bookkeeping:** `extra` (untagged artists swept into addressable content at save) and `group` (a manifest-only container for sibling parts, such as all the x tick labels)

A role fixes *what* a part is, not how it is drawn: every part also carries an editing `kind` (`line`, `shape`, `text`, `container`), so the `mean` of a box plot or fluxbox is a line while a meanmark's `mean` is a shape whose fill and stroke edit separately.

Science is unbounded (heatmaps, networks, brain maps), so the vocabulary is a **versioned core plus a
namespaced extension mechanism**: anything unrecognized becomes an `x-…` role. An unknown role still
gets a stable id and still renders and is still addressable — at worst it's a clean, tagged, editable
figure. The standard only ever *adds* power; it never makes a plot worse than a plain SVG.

## 3D scene bundles {#scene3d}

A 3D bundle contains `name.glb`, `name.fluxplot.json` and `name.recipe.json`. The scene manifest uses `spec: "fluxplot/scene3d"` and its own schema version; it is distinct from the 2D manifest. It records the source GLB hash, physical size, named parts, axes, layout, view, value fields and shape-state information.

GLB assets accepted by Flux may be prepared for rendering. The saved asset hash identifies those accepted bytes; the placement's original-source hash binds its scene metadata. A mismatch keeps the accepted mesh while refusing incompatible metadata. Import and relink through Flux to keep these records coherent.

Values and validity masks travel with the mesh, so changing a colour range does not require analysis to run again. A shape state reuses exactly the same vertex count and triangle indices. Separate morph partners also need matching names and topology. See [3D plots](/docs/3d-plots.html) for authoring and validation.

The complete machine-readable definitions are maintained with the implementation: [2D schemas](https://github.com/fluxsci/fluxplot/tree/main/schema) and [3D binary contract](https://github.com/fluxsci/fluxplot/blob/main/docs/SCENE3D_CONTRACT.md).
